title: Getting something from Miles Davis and the younger trumpeters
summary: He listens to Miles, Fats Navarro, Lee Morgan and others, saying he gets something from every trumpeter and that you cannot put them down without knowing why.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Do you like what Miles is doing these days?

Some of it yes, yes. I listen to Miles things. I get something out of his. There's something I can get out of everybody. All trumpet players, a little something. I get a lot of things from Miles. Maybe that the ordinary person, listening, would overlook, it'll just go through one ear and out the other.
But you have to dig down into the

bowels of the -- of what these guys are doing. To get -- see what they're trying -- they know what they're doing. They know what they're trying to do and they know where -- so many of us will not understand it, will not get it. But I listen to Miles, I've always listened to Miles. And I get something out of his -- in fact Herbie Mann told me one day, and -- in Dakar, Africa, we were rehearsing and I was playing like Miles, and he said you sound like Miles Davis. I got a big kick out of it, because I can imitate Miles to a certain extent, a little bit, I can. And I think there's something I get out of him, out of all trumpet players, Miles and everybody else.
And one guy I like very much, what was his name, he was killed, down in the Village, shot, what was his name?
Oh, oh, I know who you're talking about, he was shot at Art Slugs.
Yeah. I did -- I admired that guy. His playing.
And I'm sorry what happened to him, I didn't get a chance to see him more often. But I listened to a lot of his recordings. He's great. And Fats Navarro and

Yeah. I get something out of those guys and I think it's important. Because you can't put them down, unless you know what you're putting them down for. Of course, Dizzy, too. Dizzy -- get a big kick out of him.
